title: Global publics still see the UN as necessary but want visible delivery, outward-facing leadership, and a break with institutional habit
source_unit: United Nations Foundation and GeoPoll, A Mandate for Renewal: Global Public Opinion on the United Nations and the Selection of the 10th Secretary-General
geography: 20 countries representing 56% of the world's population, including all permanent and elected UN Security Council members

observations.period: September 1-16, 2026 fieldwork; public assessment of UN relevance and delivery

denominator.unit: citizens surveyed across 20 countries, 250 per country, using mobile web and computer-assisted telephone interviewing

un_necessary.unit: percent saying the United Nations remains necessary today

un_delivery_struggle.unit: percent saying the UN remains necessary but is struggling to deliver results

un_outdated.unit: percent viewing the UN as outdated and no longer necessary

delivery_legitimacy_gap.value: Institutional relevance remains high while confidence in visible delivery is conditional and frustrated.

observations.method: GeoPoll fielded a 20-country survey from September 1-16, 2026, with 250 respondents per country using mobile web and computer-assisted telephone interviewing.
observations.uncertainty: The small equal-country samples limit within-country subgroup analysis; mobile/web access may skew the sample toward more digitally connected populations, and the sponsor frames the survey around UN renewal.
observations.subgroup: Countries include the five permanent Security Council members, ten elected members serving in 2026, and five major powers outside the Council; within-country subgroup data are not reported.
observations.counterinterpretation: Saying the UN is necessary may express preference for some international system rather than confidence in the UN's current institutional form or specific programs.

observations.period: September 2026; global priorities for an outward-facing UN

conflict_prevention.unit: percent selecting preventing and ending armed conflicts among their top three priorities for global cooperation

poverty_inequality.unit: percent selecting reducing poverty and inequality among their top three priorities

climate_action.unit: percent selecting climate action among their top three priorities

priority_route.value: Public demand for the next UN leader is organized around external crisis response and daily-life stakes rather than internal institutional reform alone.

observations.method: Priority-ranking questions in the GeoPoll survey; respondents selected up to three global cooperation priorities.
observations.uncertainty: Ranked priorities do not reveal willingness to finance, deploy, compromise, or accept trade-offs among conflict prevention, poverty, climate, rights, and economic management.
observations.subgroup: 20-country public sample; country-level detail is available through the report materials but is not fully reproduced in the release.
observations.counterinterpretation: Security-first priorities could support multilateral prevention, national militarization, border restriction, or other divergent policy routes.

observations.period: September 2026; preferred leadership role and public visibility

outward_diplomat.unit: percent preferring the next Secretary-General to be primarily a diplomat who can help end wars

crisis_manager.unit: percent preferring a crisis manager for global emergencies

moral_voice.unit: percent preferring a moral voice to speak out on human rights and existential threats

internal_reform.unit: percent preferring a leader focused primarily on internal reform

race_awareness.unit: percent having heard little or nothing about the Secretary-General selection

visibility_gap.value: The public wants visible external action while the leadership selection itself remains largely outside public attention.

observations.method: Descriptive role-preference and awareness questions in the GeoPoll survey.
observations.uncertainty: Role labels are broad and may carry different meanings across languages and political contexts; low race awareness does not establish low interest once a selection is made.
observations.subgroup: 20-country public sample; within-country subgroup results are not reported in the release.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low awareness may reflect the timing and technicality of the selection process rather than a durable public disengagement from global leadership.

observations.period: September 2026; gender, generation, and North-South legitimacy signals

woman_secretary_general_importance.unit: percent saying it is important for the next Secretary-General to be a woman

women_support.unit: percent among women saying a woman Secretary-General is important

young_adult_support.unit: percent among adults ages 18-34 saying a woman Secretary-General is important

global_south_support.unit: percent among respondents in the Global South saying a woman Secretary-General is important

institutional_trust_gap.value: Trust in international institutions to make progress is reported at 65% in the Global South versus 44% in the Global North.

representation_route.value: Leadership legitimacy is tied to both visible delivery and who is perceived to represent the institution's future.

observations.method: Gender, age, and regional subgroup comparisons reported from the GeoPoll sample.
observations.uncertainty: The release does not report the full cross-tabulation, country composition of Global North/South groups, or causal effects of leader identity on trust and performance.
observations.subgroup: Women, adults ages 18-34, and respondents grouped into Global North and Global South categories.
observations.counterinterpretation: Support for a woman leader can reflect a desire for change, representation, or institutional renewal without implying agreement on policy or performance.

related_sources.claim: The official UN Foundation report page provides the report framing, key findings, and downloadable report materials.
The distributed UN Foundation release provides sample design, fieldwork dates, limitations, and headline results.

boundary: This record adds a leadership-transition and multilateral-legitimacy route: publics see the UN as necessary but condition delivery, crisis response, visibility, and representation. It does not establish future Secretary-General performance, causal effects of leader identity, country-level public opinion beyond the reported sample, or actual UN delivery outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The UN Foundation official report page and publisher-distributed GeoPoll release were reviewed for sample design, fieldwork, limits, UN necessity and delivery, priorities, leadership role preferences, selection awareness, gender, age, and Global North/South comparisons.
